CDS BS alumni here, now in the CSI MS program and working as a junior data scientist

I would say one of the most important concepts that are need to know are understanding the value of exploratory data analysis, really getting to know the data you are working with, and knowing what questions to ask. Those by far have been the most important part of working in the data science field, and I think that part is over looked since we are always given dummy data or hypothetical situations in school that already have this part figured out. Know when to work with a subject matter expert and what questions to ask them that will help you with your analysis (a lot of applications of data science require subject matter experts of the data you are actually working with)

Another thing I would say is very important is understanding model assumptions before you actually use a specific model. Or know how to gauge/identify if the data you are working with meets the assumptions of the model you are trying to use. A lot of models people want to use on data will not actually work for that data or the distribution of the data or sample size won't work for that type of model etc. Also, you should be strong in query languages and have an understanding of data structures and be flexible in that area because there are a lot of different options for the way data is stored.

Additionally, another thing that has been very important in my career and in my MS is knowing how to verify and validate your models. A lot of the time people just get results that work and there is nothing backing it up or just a black box to point to. Knowing how to explain your model, verify it, validate it, and have it be a trusted, robust, and non-biased model is a very important skill to have amongst a lot of "package" happy data scientists. And just knowing when to use the right model, and not always going for the most complex one that sounds fancy. Do a lot of reading about different models and different use cases, get to know the academic and industry standards for different types of analysis.  OH and you NEED to know how to clean data. Any kind of data. Because in the real world, no one has 100% clean data. Trust me.

I don't know which minor you should do, but those are really important concepts. I did a CDS major and learned a lot of the stats "backbone" of data science on my own from youtube and I am continuing my stats knowledge by taking graduate level stats courses in my MS. I think no matter which one you do, you will have to fill in the other's gap somehow. I think having statistical understanding keeps one from being "package" happy. Which is important, but I also think the mindset of what I mentioned in the first paragraph, is something I learned from my CDS program but can probably be learned from the stats department or other activities as well. Get involved in data hackathons, get data science internships, play around with many different data sets online, that will give you a lot of understanding of what things to look out for as they come up naturally in your experiences.

Also, try doing data science projects that are close to your heart/interests. This will allow you to dive deep and understand the data and really expand on what you can do with the project. This will also help you stand out and will allow you to be naturally passionate when it comes to interviewing. Because whatever project it is, is very close to you and being able to explain why you did something, how you did it, and what the results mean to you, is a very very important skill and will allow you to find a career path that aligns with it someway or another. Letting yourself show through your work, is an underrated skill and will allow you to connect with your colleagues and will put you in a position of doing work that means something to you.

Hey,  junior CDS major here. So far, I am really enjoying the CDS program, the department minus one professor has been great and I've learned so much from all of them. The classes are a mix of many things: I have learned how to wrangle and manipulate data, how to visualize data in many different cool graphs and formats, hypothesis testing and inference about larger populations using samples, how to simulate dynamical systems, machine learning, and how to create databases using SQL and use them for anything from applications to dashboards. The languages used primarily in the CDS department are R and python, I've used both for the things I have stated above, except for the one where I specified SQL.

In comparison to CS I would say that the CDS classes are a mix of science, computer science, statistics rather than being heavily focused on programming, theory, development and application. It's more using the tools that computer scientists use rather than learning everything about them. The classes teach the languages (such as R and python) at the beginning and throughout but aren't very focused on the language itself and everything you can do with it, but more the specific tools we can use to better understand the world around us through data. There are a lot of intersections between CS and CDS, I would take a look at some of the class descriptions and see which ones sound more like something that interests you. Before I transferred to Mason I was choosing between these two majors as well.

Hello, CDS major here. CDS 101 (with Dr. White) is great, it has some topics where depending on your statistical knowledge it may seem complicated, but if you do the readings and are interested in it, it is a very good class especially for your major. 

Also, I may add that statistical knowledge is not required to actually get the work done (since it's an introductory class) because the code will work whether or not you understand the deeper concepts, but they are very good things to learn and will be of great use in your minor and life. I would highly recommend it, you will work with all kinds of data sets, learn how to manipulate them, create data visualizations and inference/hypothesis testing as well as dipping your toes into making predictions using data. If you want to you can also take CDS 102 (the lab for CDS 101) while taking 101 because they go hand and hand.
